title: Message experiments lab notes — eng trio
content:
Purpose:
Quick iteration lab for persona-targeted messaging (ML engineers, backend engineers, platform teams). Build concise talk tracks, competitive hooks + technical proof points, and 3 tactical experiments we can run with sales and content next quarter. Notes are intentionally raw — use for scripts, AB test variants, and playbook snippets.

Context / assumptions:
- Buyers are pragmatic engineers: no fluff. They want measurable SLOs, cost math, and reproducible benchmarks.
- Messaging must map to operational primitives they care about: latency percentiles, cost per 1k tokens, failure modes, rollback flow, and infra ownership boundaries.
- Competitive landscape: managed endpoints (big clouds), vertical LLM APIs, and self-hosted inference runtimes.

High-level framing (single sentence per persona):
- ML engineer: "Ship model-driven features that match research latency/cost assumptions — without rebuilding infra — by leveraging a runtime that preserves KV caching, supports quantized variants, and plugs into your evals."
- Backend engineer: "Add LLM endpoints with predictable latency and cost controls (batching + cache) so product SLAs don't regress when traffic spikes."
- Platform team: "Standardize inference across teams with RBAC'd Private deployments, autoscaling reservation primitives, and unified observability so you can govern spend and uptime."

Three short demo hooks (30s each):
1) Latency-respect demo (for backend): show identical prompt served from two configs (naive single-request vs Redwood smart batching + cache) — display p50/p95 delta and token cost.
2) Migration micro-play (for ML engineers): show a quick switch from local GPU to Redwood Dedicated; same model/version, canary rollout, and quality regression check via eval set.
3) Governance snapshot (for platform): show Console route controls, per-team quotas, and billing breakdown for a simulated spike.

Talk tracks and scripts (30–60s snippets):
ML engineer script: "You're iterating on a new assistant model and worried inference artifacts — like KV cache behavior and quantization — will change quality. With Redwood you keep the same model checkpoint and get a serving profile that guarantees KV-preserving inference and exposes quantization options per-route. That means you can test 4x cheaper variants while running your evals side-by-side; if metrics degrade, roll back automatically."
Backend engineer script: "Your app needs predictable tail latency. Redwood's routing primitives let you pin a low-latency pool, apply workload-aware batching, and set a fallback model variant if capacity is constrained. We show you real p95 and request-level traces so you can instrument SLOs in minutes."
Platform team script: "You manage teams, not single endpoints. Redwood Private gives you tenant isolation, API key policy controls, and a console with per-route cost attribution. Set reservations for seasonal traffic and routes that require guaranteed throughput — then enforce via RBAC and audit logs."

Key technical proof points to include on sell sheets: (short bullets for engineers)
- KV cache compatibility: exact replay fidelity for cached prefixes; works with instruction-tuned chat models.
- Continuous batching: maintains p50 while increasing throughput by Xx (include lab numbers in datasheet).
- Quantization matrix: per-model profiles (8-bit/4-bit) + expected loss in perplexity/latency tradeoffs.
- Deterministic rollouts: canary by traffic % + automatic fallback to older model variants.
- Observability: token-level cost, trace links to request IDs, per-route token histogram.

Competitive differentiators (short calling cards):
- Versus big cloud managed endpoints: deeper inference controls (KV, batching knobs, quant profiles) + transparent unit economics (not opaque pricing buckets).
- Versus pure self-hosted runtimes: we provide a unified control plane + dev-friendly SDKs so teams avoid one-off ops debt.
- Versus LLM-API vendors that emphasize features: we emphasize operational predictability and cost levers at scale.

Common objections and quick rebuttals (cheat sheet):
- "We can just run this in k8s ourselves." Rebuttal: "True for prototypes; at scale, tenant isolation, fine-grained autoscaling for heterogeneous models, and cost telemetry require nontrivial infra + SRE costs — typical time to ship is 6–12 months with recurring maintenance. Redwood offloads that and provides model-aware optimizations out of the box."
- "We care about data privacy, can you do VPC/on-prem?" Rebuttal: "Yes — Private deployments run behind customer-controlled VPCs and support KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs; we also offer an on-prem package for air-gapped requirements."
- "What about hallucinations and quality regression?" Rebuttal: "We tie rollouts to eval suites; you can define regression gates that block canaries and trigger fallback. We also provide telemetry to triage degenerate prompts."

Message calibration matrix (short form):
- Signal: latency percentiles, cost-per-1k tokens, rollback time, reproducible eval pass/fail.
- Noise to avoid: broad claims about "better quality" without evals; marketing buzzwords.

Three experiment ideas to run in next 6 weeks (owner, hypothesis, metric):
1) Sales script AB test — "cost-first vs reliability-first"
   - Owner: Priya Shah
   - Hypothesis: Backend engineers respond better to demos that show p95 improvements; ML engineers respond better to tests showing quality-preserving quantization.
   - Primary metric: demo-to-POC conversion rate (by persona).

2) Landing page microcopy experiment — "batching explainer vs simple latency chart"
   - Owner: Ethan Rivera
   - Hypothesis: Platform buyers click-through more with governance controls emphasized; ML buyers click more when there is quantization matrix + sample eval.
   - Primary metric: persona-segmented clicks to docs and demo requests.

3) One-pager technical brief vs short-slide deck for SE outreach
   - Owner: Maya Patel
   - Hypothesis: SEs get better traction with one-pager containing command snippets and p95 tables.
   - Primary metric: time-to-first-POC and meeting-agreement rate.

Quick measurements we should capture during demos / POC:
- p50/p95/p99 latency under production-like qps
- tokens-per-second and cost per 1k tokens across model variants (FP16, 8-bit, 4-bit)
- rollout time (seconds to shift traffic) and time to rollback
- amber/critical error rate and graceful-degradation events
- console trace -> request-id linking for 3 sample requests

Open questions / TODOs (notes-to-self):
- Pull latest Dedicated latency bench (Jul 2025) and add a one-line frame with numbers. (ACTION: Liam)
- Build a 2-slide demo variant for backend persona that shows an actual trace and timeline. (ACTION: Maya)
- Draft a short shell script snippet that runs local eval set against hosted and dedicated variants and prints delta. Include in one-pager. (ACTION: Priya)
- Validate phrasing around "KV-preserving" with infra team — some models have cache semantics that change with kernel optimizations. (ACTION: Eng-serving-runtime)

Appendix: rough demo checklist (non-exhaustive)
- Start console with two routes: route-A (low-latency pool) and route-B (default pool)
- Preload KV cache for route-A with common prefixes used in demo prompts
- Run a scripted traffic generator (10–50rps) and capture p95
- Swap route traffic 50% -> 100% to simulate gradual rollout
- Trigger quantized variant and run eval set
- Capture screenshots: token cost dashboard, trace detail, rollout timeline

Notes-to-self (raw):
- Keep this doc short and evolving — prefer iterative bullets over final prose.
- Make sure we have one canonical datasheet for each demo variant (link above).
